My top five changes in Python 3.14 versus 3.13, ranked by practical impact:

1. **Deferred type annotations by default.** Annotations are evaluated when needed, rather than when functions, classes, or modules are defined. This reduces definition-time work and makes forward references easier. The new `annotationlib` supports runtime inspection. Libraries that inspect annotations should review compatibility. [Official notes](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-deferred-annotations)

2. **Free-threaded Python becomes officially supported.** The optional build that can run without the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) moves beyond its experimental status in 3.13, with performance improvements. It enables parallel Python threads, but remains optional; dependency compatibility still matters. [Official notes](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-free-threaded-now-supported)

3. **Multiple interpreters get standard-library APIs.** `concurrent.interpreters` and `InterpreterPoolExecutor` expose isolated interpreters within one process, enabling multicore execution. They require explicit data exchange, and some third-party extensions remain incompatible. [Official notes](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-multiple-interpreters)

4. **Template strings arrive: `t"Hello {name}"`.** Unlike f-strings, t-strings produce a structured `Template` object that keeps literal text and interpolated values separate. Custom processors can use this for escaping, logging, and other formatting; t-strings do not automatically sanitize input. [Official notes](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-template-string-literals)

5. **Built-in Zstandard compression.** The new `compression.zstd` module adds Zstandard compression and decompression, with archive support in `tarfile`, `zipfile`, and `shutil`. This removes the need for a third-party package for common Zstandard tasks. [Official notes](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-zstandard)

|---|---:|

| Global, sandbox | **25 requests/second per account** |

Anthropic’s [“Building effective agents”](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) argues that **successful AI systems usually start simple and add complexity only when it measurably improves results.**

The article distinguishes **workflows**, where code defines the steps, from **agents**, where the model decides which steps and tools to use. Workflows suit predictable tasks; agents suit open-ended problems whose solution path cannot be specified in advance. Often, a single well-designed model call with retrieval and examples is enough.

It describes five reusable workflow patterns:

- **Prompt chaining:** Complete a task through sequential steps, with checks between them.
- **Routing:** Send each request to the appropriate specialist model or process.
- **Parallelization:** Run independent subtasks—or multiple attempts—simultaneously.
- **Orchestrator-workers:** Have a central model dynamically delegate subtasks and combine results.
- **Evaluator-optimizer:** Improve an output through repeated evaluation and revision.

For autonomous agents, the essential loop is **act, observe real results, and adjust**. Tool outputs and test results help the agent track progress. Human checkpoints, stopping conditions, and sandbox testing help control costs and errors.

A major practical lesson is that **tool design deserves as much attention as prompting**: clear descriptions, intuitive parameters, examples, and formats that make mistakes harder. Frameworks can help, but developers should understand their underlying behavior.

The article’s guiding principles are simplicity, transparency, and carefully documented and tested tools. Coding and customer support are promising applications because success can be measured and feedback can guide improvement.

| Item | Neon Free | Supabase Free | PlanetScale Postgres |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | [$0/month](https://neon.com/pricing) | [$0/month](https://supabase.com/pricing) | No free plan; single-node Postgres starts at [$5/month](https://planetscale.com/docs/planetscale-plans#free-plan) |

| Compute | [100 CU-hours/month per project; sizes up to 2 CU, with 8 GB RAM](https://neon.com/pricing) | [Shared CPU, 500 MB RAM](https://supabase.com/pricing); no monthly compute-hour allowance listed | No free allowance |
| Outbound transfer | [5 GB per project included](https://neon.com/pricing) | [5 GB egress plus a separate 5 GB cached-egress allowance](https://supabase.com/pricing) | No free allowance |
| Inactivity | Scales to zero after [5 minutes](https://neon.com/pricing) | Free projects pause after [1 week of inactivity](https://supabase.com/pricing) | No free tier |
| Database branching | [10 included branches per project](https://neon.com/pricing) | Not included on [Free](https://supabase.com/pricing) | No free allowance |
| Recovery | Instant restore covering up to [6 hours or 1 GB of data changes; 1 snapshot](https://neon.com/pricing) | Automatic backups and point-in-time recovery aren’t included on [Free](https://supabase.com/pricing) | No free allowance |

A few distinctions matter:

- **Neon’s compute allowance measures usage, not uptime.** CU-hours combine compute size and running time; autoscaling changes consumption, and scaling to zero saves the allowance. Its maximum compute size isn’t something you can run continuously for free. [Neon’s explanation](https://neon.com/pricing)
- **Supabase’s quotas have different scopes.** Database size is per project, while usage quotas such as egress, file storage and authentication are shared across the organization. The active-project limit applies across organizations. [Supabase billing documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/billing-on-supabase)
- **Both now bundle backend services.** Neon lists [60,000 monthly active auth users and 5 GB object storage](https://neon.com/pricing). Supabase includes [50,000 monthly active auth users, 1 GB file storage and 500,000 Edge Function invocations](https://supabase.com/pricing). These storage allowances are separate from database storage.

For database experiments and branching, I’d choose **Neon**: its free tier offers more projects and database storage. For an app built around Supabase’s integrated APIs, Auth, Storage and Realtime, **Supabase** remains a useful free starting point. **PlanetScale requires a paid budget**.

Anthropic’s guidance centers on **clear triggers, concise instructions, and testing against real tasks**. Here are the main practices:

- **Make discovery explicit.** Give the skill a specific name and a description explaining both what it does and when to use it. Include phrases users are likely to say.
- **Keep `SKILL.md` focused.** Assume Claude knows general concepts. Include your workflow, domain rules, and conventions; aim for fewer than 500 lines.
- **Load details only when needed.** Put extensive references, examples, and scripts in supporting files. Link them directly from `SKILL.md`, avoid chains of nested references, and add a contents list to reference files longer than 100 lines.
- **Match precision to the task.** Give judgment tasks flexible guidance, recurring outputs a template, and fragile operations exact commands or tested scripts.
- **Define completion clearly.** Use ordered steps for complex workflows, concrete input/output examples, and validation loops: check → fix → check again.
- **Prefer scripts for repeatable operations.** Bundle reliable utilities, document dependencies and errors, and state whether Claude should execute a script or read it as reference.
- **Test before expanding.** Start with at least three representative scenarios and measure performance without the skill. Add minimal instructions to address observed failures, then retest in fresh sessions and across intended models. These recommendations come from [Anthropic’s authoring guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices).

For **Claude Code specifically**, store shared project skills at `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` and personal skills at `~/.claude/skills/`. Set `disable-model-invocation: true` for workflows you want to trigger manually, such as deployments. Test both `/skill-name` invocation and whether natural requests activate the right skill. See the [Claude Code skills documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills).

A web crawler is a program that automatically visits web pages and follows links to discover more pages. Search engines use crawlers to gather information so pages can appear in search results.

```python
from urllib.parse import urljoin

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup


def extract_links(url: str) -> list[str]:
    """Download a webpage and return its links as absolute URLs."""
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
    response.raise_for_status()

    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")
    return [
        urljoin(response.url, anchor["href"])
        for anchor in soup.find_all("a", href=True)
    ]


links = extract_links("https://example.com")
print(links)
```

| Data location | Usually URL query parameters, such as `/search?q=cats` | Usually the request body, such as JSON or form data |
| Expected effect | Should not change server state | May change server state |
| Repeating a request | Should have the same intended effect as making it once | May cause duplicate actions, such as creating two orders |
| Caching | Commonly cached | Usually not cached |

For example:

```http
GET /products/42
```

Fetches product 42.

```http
POST /products
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "Notebook", "price": 5}
```

Asks the server to create a product.

**POST is not inherently more secure than GET.** HTTPS encrypts both in transit, but GET parameters appear in URLs and may be recorded in browser history and logs. Avoid putting passwords or other secrets in URLs.

**Scraping** extracts content from a specific web page, such as a product’s name and price.

**Crawling** discovers and visits pages by following links, such as finding all product pages in an online store.

They often work together: a crawler finds the pages, and a scraper extracts the information from each one.

My top five changes in Python 3.14 compared with 3.13, ranked by their impact on everyday development and concurrency:

1. **Type annotations are evaluated lazily by default.** In 3.13, annotations normally evaluate when functions or classes are defined; 3.14 defers evaluation until needed. This simplifies forward references and reduces definition-time work. The new `annotationlib` supports runtime inspection; libraries that read annotations may need updates. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-deferred-annotations)

2. **Free-threaded Python becomes officially supported.** The optional build that can run without the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) moves beyond its experimental status in 3.13, with substantial performance improvements. This enables parallel Python threads, though dependency compatibility still matters. The standard build retains the GIL. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-free-threaded-now-supported)

3. **Multiple interpreters get standard-library APIs.** New `concurrent.interpreters` and `InterpreterPoolExecutor` make isolated interpreters accessible from Python code, enabling CPU work across multiple cores within one process. Data sharing requires explicit coordination, and some extension modules remain incompatible. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-multiple-interpreters)

4. **Template strings arrive: `t"Hello {name}"`.** Unlike an f-string, a t-string produces a `Template` object that preserves literal text and interpolated values separately. Custom processors can then apply context-specific escaping or formatting; t-strings do not automatically make output safe. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-template-string-literals)

5. **Zstandard compression joins the standard library.** New `compression.zstd` provides compression and decompression without a third-party Python package. Zstandard support also extends to archive handling in `tarfile`, `zipfile`, and `shutil`. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-zstandard)

Anthropic’s [“Building effective agents”](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) argues that **simple, well-tested designs usually beat complex agent frameworks**. Start with a single LLM call, supported by retrieval or tools, and add complexity only when evaluations show it improves results.

The article distinguishes two approaches:

- **Workflows:** Code defines the steps. Best for predictable, well-defined tasks.
- **Agents:** The model decides which steps and tools to use. Best for open-ended tasks whose path cannot be specified in advance.

It describes five reusable workflow patterns:

| Pattern | What it does |
|---|---|
| Prompt chaining | Breaks a task into sequential steps, with checks between them. |
| Routing | Sends each request to the appropriate specialized process or model. |
| Parallelization | Runs independent subtasks or multiple assessments simultaneously. |
| Orchestrator-workers | Lets a central model identify subtasks, delegate them, and combine results. |
| Evaluator-optimizer | Repeatedly improves an output using another model’s feedback. |

For autonomous agents, the core mechanism is a **tool-use feedback loop**: act, observe real results, and adjust. These systems need clear stopping conditions, testing, and appropriate human oversight because costs and errors can accumulate.

A major practical lesson is to **treat tool design as seriously as prompt design**. Clear descriptions, straightforward parameters, examples, and formats that prevent mistakes can substantially improve reliability.

The article highlights customer support and coding as promising applications because both combine actions with measurable outcomes and useful feedback. Its guiding principles are simplicity, transparency, and carefully documented and tested tools.

3. **Load details only when needed.** Put the core workflow in `SKILL.md`; move lengthy examples, schemas, and reference material into separate files. Link those files directly from `SKILL.md`, explain when to read them, and avoid chains of nested references. [Authoring guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

4. **Match precision to risk.** Give flexible guidance for tasks with several valid approaches, such as code review. Give exact commands and ordering for fragile operations, such as migrations. Provide one sensible default and explain the exceptions. [Authoring guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

5. **Define the workflow and what success looks like.** Use clear steps, concrete input/output examples, and validation criteria. For complex tasks, include a checklist and a “validate → fix → validate again” loop. [Authoring guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

6. **Bundle scripts for repeatable operations.** Tested scripts improve consistency and avoid regenerating the same code. State dependencies, document inputs and outputs, handle errors clearly, and distinguish “run this script” from “read this as reference.” [Authoring guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

7. **Choose invocation behavior deliberately.** In Claude Code, use `disable-model-invocation: true` for workflows you want users to start explicitly, such as deployments. Store shared project skills at `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`; personal skills go under `~/.claude/skills/`. [Claude Code skills documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills)

8. **Test before expanding the instructions.** Start with at least three representative scenarios and compare performance with and without the skill. Test automatic activation as well as task completion, use fresh sessions, and check every model you intend to support. Refine instructions around observed failures. [Authoring guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

The practical takeaway: **capture a workflow that already works, add only the knowledge Claude needs, and improve it through observed use.**

**GET retrieves data; POST submits data for processing.**

| | GET | POST |
|---|---|---|
| Typical use | Fetch a page, search results, or a record | Submit a form, create a record, or upload a file |
| Where data goes | Usually in URL query parameters | Usually in the request body |
| Expected effect | Should not change server state | May change server state |
| Repeating a request | Should have the same intended effect as sending it once | May produce additional effects, such as duplicate orders |
| Caching | Commonly cached | Less commonly cached |

Examples:

```http
GET /products?category=books
```

Requests products in the “books” category.

```http
POST /orders
Content-Type: application/json

{"productId": 42, "quantity": 2}
```

Submits an order for processing.

**POST is not inherently more secure than GET.** HTTPS encrypts both, but URLs can appear in browser history and logs, so sensitive data should not go in query parameters.

**Scraping** extracts information from a web page, such as product names, prices, or article text.

**Crawling** discovers and visits pages by following links, often across an entire website.

For example:

- **Scraping:** Read a product page and extract its price.
- **Crawling:** Follow a store’s category links to find all its product pages.

They often work together: a crawler finds the pages, and a scraper extracts the data from each one.

My top five changes in **Python 3.14 versus 3.13**, ranked by their impact on everyday development and concurrency:

1. **Type annotations are evaluated lazily by default.** In 3.13, annotations normally evaluated when a function or class was defined; 3.14 defers evaluation until needed. This reduces definition-time work and makes forward references easier. The new `annotationlib` supports runtime inspection. Libraries that inspect annotations may need adjustments. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-deferred-annotations)

2. **Free-threaded Python becomes officially supported.** The optional build that can run Python threads without the global interpreter lock (GIL) moves beyond its experimental status in 3.13, with improved performance. This enables CPU-bound threads to execute in parallel, although dependency compatibility still matters. **The standard build retains the GIL.** [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-free-threaded-now-supported)

3. **Multiple interpreters become accessible from Python code.** New `concurrent.interpreters` and `concurrent.futures.InterpreterPoolExecutor` APIs expose isolated interpreters within one process. They offer another route to multicore parallelism, with explicit communication between interpreters rather than ordinary shared state. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-multiple-interpreters)

4. **Template strings introduce `t"..."` syntax.** Unlike f-strings, a t-string such as `t"Hello {name}"` produces a `Template` object that preserves literal text and interpolated values separately. Custom processors can inspect and escape values before producing HTML, SQL, or other output; t-strings do not automatically make output safe. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-template-string-literals)

5. **Zstandard compression joins the standard library.** New `compression.zstd` provides Zstandard compression and decompression without a third-party Python package. Zstandard support also extends to archive handling through `tarfile`, `zipfile`, and `shutil`. [Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-zstandard)

Anthropic’s [“Building effective agents”](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) argues that **the best agent systems start simple and add complexity only when it measurably improves results.**

The article distinguishes two approaches:

- **Workflows:** Code defines the steps, while LLMs perform specific tasks. Best for predictable, well-defined work.
- **Agents:** The LLM decides which steps and tools to use, adapting to results. Best for open-ended problems where the path cannot be specified in advance.

It describes five reusable workflow patterns:

| Pattern | What it does |
|---|---|
| Prompt chaining | Breaks a task into sequential steps, with checks between them. |
| Routing | Sends each input to a specialized prompt, model, or process. |
| Parallelization | Runs independent subtasks or multiple attempts simultaneously. |
| Orchestrator-workers | Uses a central LLM to identify subtasks, delegate them, and combine results. |
| Evaluator-optimizer | Repeatedly generates, critiques, and improves an answer. |

Autonomous agents extend these ideas into a loop: **choose an action, use a tool, observe the result, and adjust.** They need reliable environmental feedback, stopping conditions, testing, and appropriate human oversight because costs and errors can accumulate.

A major practical lesson is that **tool design deserves as much attention as prompting**. Clear descriptions, intuitive parameters, examples, and formats that prevent mistakes improve reliability. Frameworks can help, but developers should understand their underlying behavior and avoid unnecessary abstraction.

The authors highlight customer support and coding as promising applications because both combine actions with observable outcomes and feedback. Their advice throughout: start with a strong single LLM call, evaluate it, and introduce workflows or autonomy when the evidence justifies it.

Anthropic’s guidance emphasizes **clear triggers, concise instructions, and testing against real tasks**. The main best practices are:

1. **Write the description for discovery.** Say what the skill does and when Claude should use it. Include terms users naturally say, such as “review staged changes” or “analyze .xlsx files.” In Claude Code, frontmatter fields are optional, but `description` is recommended. [Claude Code configuration guidance](https://academy.claude.com/courses/introduction-to-agent-skills/configuration-and-multi-file-skills)

2. **Keep `SKILL.md` focused.** Include knowledge Claude needs for your workflow; skip explanations of things it already knows. Aim for fewer than 500 lines. Move detailed references into separate files and explicitly say when to read them. Keep reference links one level deep. [Authoring best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

3. **Match precision to risk.** Give flexible guidance for judgment tasks, such as reviews. Provide exact commands and sequences for fragile operations. Choose a default approach and explain exceptions instead of listing many alternatives. [Authoring best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

4. **Define the workflow and success criteria.** Use clear steps, concrete input/output examples, and templates where format matters. Include a validation loop: perform the work, check it, fix failures, then verify again. [Authoring best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

5. **Put repeatable operations in scripts.** Bundle tested utilities for consistent transformations or validation. State whether Claude should *run* a script or *read* it. Execution can save context because only its output needs to be loaded. [Multi-file skills guidance](https://academy.claude.com/courses/introduction-to-agent-skills/configuration-and-multi-file-skills)

6. **Test before expanding.** Start with representative tasks Claude struggles with, establish a baseline, then add minimal instructions. Test in fresh sessions and across intended models; refine based on missed triggers, skipped steps, and incorrect outputs. [Authoring best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

7. **Scope tool permissions deliberately.** `allowed-tools` pre-approves tools; it does **not** restrict the skill to those tools. Prefer narrow command patterns over broad `Bash` access. from urllib.parse import urljoin

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup


def extract_links(url: str) -> list[str]:
    """Download a webpage and return its anchor URLs, resolved to absolute URLs."""
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
    response.raise_for_status()

    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")
    return [
        urljoin(response.url, anchor["href"])
        for anchor in soup.find_all("a", href=True)
    ]


links = extract_links("https://example.com")
for link in links:

Matches URLs starting with `http://` or `https://` up to whitespace or common delimiters. Use case-insensitive mode to also match `HTTP://`.

**GET retrieves data; POST submits data for processing.**

| | GET | POST |
|---|---|---|
| Typical use | Fetch a page or search results | Submit a form or create a record |
| Data location | Usually URL query parameters, such as `?q=cats` | Usually the request body |
| Expected effect | Reads data without changing server state | May change server state |
| Repeating a request | Should have the same intended effect | May repeat an action, such as creating another order |
| Caching | Commonly cached | Usually not cached |

For example:

```http
GET /products?category=books
```

asks for books, while:

```http
POST /orders
Content-Type: application/json

{"productId": 42, "quantity": 1}
```

submits a new order.

**POST is not inherently more secure than GET.** HTTPS encrypts both in transit. Sensitive data should stay out of URLs because URLs can appear in browser history and server logs.

**Scraping** extracts information from a webpage, such as product names, prices, or article text.

**Crawling** discovers and visits pages by following links across a website, such as finding every product page in a store.

They often work together: a crawler finds the pages, and a scraper extracts data from each one.
